questions.q: What is an ablation study, as used in LLM architecture design?
options: Training the full-size target model multiple times with different random seeds
Changing exactly one component of a system while holding everything else fixed, then measuring the effect on an outcome metric like validation loss
A method for compressing a trained model after pretraining
A technique for cleaning training data before tokenization
questions.explain: An ablation isolates the effect of one change (removing or swapping a component) by holding all other conditions fixed and comparing the resulting metric.

questions.q: Why are architecture ablations run at small scale rather than on the full-size target model?
options: Small-scale models always produce more accurate rankings
Training the full-size model multiple times to compare design choices would be prohibitively expensive, so cheap small runs are used instead
Large models cannot be ablated due to technical limitations
Ablations are purely a theoretical exercise with no training involved
questions.explain: Testing architectural choices by training the full-scale model several times would cost far too much compute, so teams use cheap, small-scale runs to compare options first.

questions.q: Which pair of attention variants are commonly ablated specifically to reduce inference-time KV-cache memory cost?
options: LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm
RoPE vs. ALiBi
Grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-query attention (MQA) vs. standard multi-head attention
ReLU vs. GELU
questions.explain: GQA and MQA reduce the number of key/value projections, trading some quality for substantially cheaper inference-time KV-cache memory compared to standard multi-head attention.

questions.q: What core assumption does the practice of small-scale ablation rely on?
options: That small models always outperform large models on every task
That the relative ranking of architectural choices observed at small scale will still hold at the full target scale
That ablation results are always identical regardless of random seed
That data mixture has no effect on model performance
questions.explain: The practice assumes ranking transfer: if A beats B at small scale, A should still beat B at the larger target scale. This usually holds for structural wins but isn't guaranteed.

questions.q: Why do teams sometimes re-validate an ablation result at a slightly larger scale before locking it in for the full run?
options: Because small-scale ablations are always wrong
Because ranking transfer across scale is not guaranteed, so a cheap re-check reduces the risk of committing an expensive run to a choice that doesn't actually hold at the target scale
Because regulations require a second validation step
Because larger ablations are always cheaper than smaller ones
questions.explain: Since the small-to-large ranking transfer assumption can break down, teams often re-validate promising ablation results at a somewhat larger scale before committing to the expensive full-size run.
